```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  eval = identical(tolower(Sys.getenv("LLMR_RUN_VIGNETTES", "false")), "true") &&
    LLMR::llm_local_ready("qwen3-0.6b")
)
```

Hosted models answer questions; they rarely show how they arrived at an
answer. A model that runs on one's own computer can show more: the probability
it assigns to every possible next token, how it continues a reply whose
beginning someone else wrote, and how probable it finds a sentence it did not
write. LLMR runs such models through [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp),
a widely used program for running language models on ordinary hardware, and
makes them available through the same `llm_config()` used for hosted
providers.

The models involved are small, under one gigabyte, and much weaker than
current hosted models. They are tools for studying how language models
behave, not substitutes for the models a study is about.

```{r}
library(LLMR)
```

## Installing a model

One call downloads what is needed: the llama.cpp server program for this
computer and the model file.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
llm_local_install("qwen3-0.6b")
```

Before downloading, the function lists each file with its size, source, and
license, and asks for agreement; a script passes `accept_license = TRUE`
instead. Every file is pinned to an exact version and checked against its
sha256, and a second call makes no network request. The files live in
`llm_local_dir()`; `llm_local_uninstall()` removes them, and
`llm_local_models()` lists the models available by name.

```{r}
llm_local_models()[, c("name", "kind", "size_mb", "license", "installed")]
```

## The model as a provider

An installed model is a provider like any other. The server starts on the
first call and stops when R exits.

```{r}
cfg <- llm_config("llamacpp", "qwen3-0.6b", temperature = 0, thinking = FALSE)
call_llm(cfg, "What is the capital of France? Answer in one sentence.")
```

`thinking = FALSE` matters for Qwen3, which otherwise reasons at length before
answering. Structured output, tools, streaming, log-probabilities, and the
tidy verbs work as they do for hosted models.

## The next-token distribution

`llm_next_token()` returns the model's probability distribution over the next
token after a context. The context is either a chat, rendered with the
model's own template, or raw text given as `prompt`.

```{r}
llm_next_token(cfg, messages = "What is the capital of France? Answer in one sentence.",
               prefill = "The capital of France is", top_n = 5)
```

These are the model's probabilities before any sampling setting acts, so they
do not depend on temperature or top-p. `full = TRUE` returns the whole
vocabulary, about 150,000 rows for Qwen3.

## Words in the model's mouth

`prefill` writes the beginning of the assistant's reply. `llm_continue()`
then shows how the model goes on from there; with `n` above one it returns a
sample of continuations from the same point.

```{r}
llm_continue(cfg, messages = "Is coffee good for you?",
             prefill = "Honestly, I am not sure, but", n = 3,
             temperature = 1, max_tokens = 30, seed = 110)[, c("sample", "continuation")]
```

Unless the configuration or the call sets them, the continuations are drawn
from the model's full distribution: temperature 1, with none of the top-k,
top-p, or min-p truncation that llama.cpp otherwise applies. The call above
sets `temperature = 1` because `cfg` fixed it at 0, which gives the single
most probable continuation. A seed makes a sample reproducible on the same llama.cpp build
and device; continuation `i` uses `seed + i - 1`.

Earlier turns can be faked as well, by passing them in `messages` with role
`"assistant"`.

## How probable is a given text?

`llm_score()` gives the log-probability of each token of a text after a
context, whether or not the model would have produced it.

```{r}
s <- llm_score(cfg, " Lyon.", prompt = "The capital of France is")
s[, c("token", "logprob", "rank")]
attr(s, "total_logprob")
```

`llm_choice_probs()` compares several continuations of the same context.
Longer options have lower total probability by construction, so options of
similar length compare most directly. Each option is written as the model
would produce it: at the start of a chat reply, without a leading space.

```{r}
llm_choice_probs(cfg, c("Yes", "No"),
                 messages = "Is Paris the capital of France? Answer yes or no.")
```

## Tokens and templates

`llm_tokenize()` and `llm_detokenize()` use the model's tokenizer, and
`llm_render_template()` shows the exact text the model reads.

```{r}
llm_tokenize(cfg, "The capital of France is Paris.")
cat(llm_render_template(cfg, "Name a color.", prefill = "My answer is"))
```

## Embeddings

Two multilingual embedding models are available by name. `bge-m3` needs no
task prefix and has strong published results for Persian and Arabic;
`embeddinggemma-2` is smaller and faster and was trained with task prefixes,
which LLMR adds from `task =` (default `"similarity"`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
llm_local_install("bge-m3")
texts <- c("The government raised the national budget for schools.",
           "دولت بودجهٔ ملی مدارس را افزایش داد.")
X <- get_batched_embeddings(texts, llm_config("llamacpp", "bge-m3"))
sum(X[1, ] * X[2, ])  # vectors are unit length, so this is the cosine
```

With `embeddinggemma-2`, `task = "search_query"` and `task = "document"` give
the asymmetric prefixes for retrieval, `task = "none"` sends the text as
written, and `dimensions = 256` truncates to one of the sizes the model was
trained for.

## Reproducibility

Each result of the token-level functions carries an attribute `llmr_local`
that records the model, the sha256 of its file, the llama.cpp build, the
device, and the exact context.

The device matters. On the same model, log-probabilities computed on a Mac's
GPU and on its CPU differ in the first decimal place (by up to about 0.2 in
tests with Qwen3 0.6B), and on the CPU they also depend on settings such as
flash attention, which LLMR turns off. Repeated requests on one device and
build give identical values, so numbers meant to be compared should come from
the same device, and on the CPU from the same type of machine. The device can
be chosen when the server starts:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
llm_local_start("qwen3-0.6b", device = "cpu", threads = 4)
```

`llm_score()` processes each prefix afresh, while the log-probabilities
reported during generation come from processing tokens one at a time; the two
differ by floating-point effects (about 1e-3 on the GPU, up to about 0.1 on
the CPU), and `cache = TRUE` reproduces the generation values. Embeddings of
the same text can differ by about 1e-3 between calls that batch it with
different texts; starting an embedding server with `parallel = 1` and
embedding texts one at a time makes them repeat exactly. Results that carry a
claim are best checked against a full-precision reference implementation of
the same model.

## Other models and systems

`llm_local_model()` describes any GGUF file on Hugging Face; its version and
checksum are read from Hugging Face at install time and recorded.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
llm_local_install(llm_local_model("Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-GGUF", "Qwen3-1.7B-Q8_0.gguf"))
```

The official llama.cpp builds run on macOS 13.3 or later, Windows with the
Microsoft Visual C++ runtime, and Linux with glibc 2.34 or later (Ubuntu 22.04,
Debian 12, RHEL 9, or newer). On older Linux systems, such as many computing
clusters, a llama.cpp built on that system can be used through
`llm_local_start(server = )`.

```{r, include = FALSE}
llm_local_stop()
```
